detail:
MCAS can produce anaphylaxis, and sources emphasize preparedness. ASCIA's 2025 position paper includes "appropriate management of anaphylaxis with adrenaline autoinjector training and Anaphylaxis Action Plan if indicated." An AJMC summary of a patient-perspective paper states that "having 2 doses of self-injectable epinephrine available at all times is required" — stated in the patient-perspective source, not as a clinical guideline.

The emphasis is not only on having epinephrine available, but on training in how to use the autoinjector and on maintaining a written action plan for when symptoms escalate.

Anaphylaxis is a medical emergency. Talk to your doctor about whether an anaphylaxis action plan and adrenaline autoinjectors are appropriate for you.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material.
sourceName: The American Journal of Managed Care (AJMC)
sourceVideoTitle: Daily life activity creates triggers in mast cell disorders
summary: Sources emphasize anaphylaxis preparedness for MCAS: autoinjector training and a written action plan (ASCIA); an AJMC summary of a patient-perspective paper states "having 2 doses of self-injectable epinephrine available at all times is required" (stated as a patient-perspective position, not a clinical guideline).
takeaways: sources stress practicing with your adrenaline autoinjector so you are ready, not just carrying it
guidelines call for a written anaphylaxis action plan for when symptoms escalate
ask your doctor if an action plan and autoinjector are right for you
title: Anaphylaxis preparedness and action plans
